who_could_be_harmed: Small farmers and food banks if forecasting shifts surplus away from donation; low-income shoppers if waste cuts come through price.
dual_use: Demand forecasting also optimizes pricing power.
bias_and_representation: Waste data mostly from rich countries; models may not transfer.
ethics: Who owns retailer data shared with charities, and who is accountable when a predicted surplus doesn't arrive.
morality: Is it right to treat hunger as a logistics problem when food is wasted because the hungry can't pay for it?
devils_advocate: Waste is a price and distribution problem, not a prediction problem. Better forecasts mainly save retailers money, and could mean less surplus is donated.

who_could_be_harmed: People in under-sensored neighborhoods if models are confident where data is thin.
dual_use: Hyperlocal risk maps can feed insurance redlining.
bias_and_representation: Sensor and report density tracks wealth, so poorer areas look safer than they are.
ethics: Who is accountable for a missed warning; consent for using health records.
morality: Is it right to put effort into adapting to harm rather than stopping emissions?
devils_advocate: Adaptation tools can make climate change feel manageable and lower pressure to cut emissions. And warnings don't help people who have nowhere cooler or drier to go.

who_could_be_harmed: Tenants flagged as high risk; people whose records are linked without consent.
dual_use: An eviction-risk score is also a tenant-screening tool for landlords.
bias_and_representation: Homelessness data undercounts youth, women and people avoiding shelters.
ethics: Consent and privacy for linked records; who sees risk scores.
morality: Is it right to predict someone's housing loss rather than guarantee housing?
devils_advocate: The shortage is a supply problem. A model doesn't build homes; it can only ration scarce ones, and may become a way to screen people out.

who_could_be_harmed: Workers in flagged sectors if employers respond with automation or cuts.
dual_use: Employers could use the same data to pay exactly the local minimum.
bias_and_representation: Informal work is missing from wage data, so the worst gaps are invisible.
ethics: Licensing and attribution for proprietary wage data; accuracy of public claims about employers.
morality: Whose definition of a decent life sets the living wage?
devils_advocate: Living-wage gaps are well documented already. The bottleneck is political will and bargaining power, which a dashboard doesn't change.

who_could_be_harmed: Teens whose online activity is monitored; families with less time or tech access, who get blamed for harm.
dual_use: Child-safety monitoring tools are also surveillance tools, for parents, schools or states.
bias_and_representation: Research and programs skew to US and English-speaking youth.
ethics: Consent and privacy for minors; who sees a young person's data and what happens when a tool flags them.
morality: Is it right to design childhood around protection from technology instead of designing technology that's safe for children?
devils_advocate: Panics about new media are old; heavy protection can cut youth off from community and information, especially LGBTQ+ and isolated kids who find support online.

who_could_be_harmed: Communities whose recordings are used without consent or who lose control of sacred or private knowledge.
dual_use: Speech and translation data for small languages can also enable surveillance of those communities.
bias_and_representation: Datasets favor languages with online text; oral-only languages and dialects are underrepresented or flattened into one 'standard'.
ethics: Data sovereignty: who owns recordings, who can license them, and whether communities can withdraw them.
morality: Is it right for outsiders, or AI companies, to decide which languages are worth saving and in what form?
devils_advocate: A language lives in its speakers, not in a dataset. Money spent on AI tools could go to speakers, teachers and immersion schools instead, and an AI that 'speaks' a language may reduce the felt need to learn it.

who_could_be_harmed: People affected by AI decisions they can't question; researchers exposed to harmful red-team content.
dual_use: Red-teaming datasets and jailbreak prompts also teach people how to break safeguards; interpretability tools can help steer models toward harm.
bias_and_representation: Safety data is mostly English and US-centered, so models 'safe' in English may not be safe in other languages.
ethics: Who gets access to frontier model internals, and who is accountable when a known failure ships anyway.
morality: Is it right to deploy systems whose reasoning we can't inspect, and does studying them legitimize deploying them?
devils_advocate: Interpretability on small open models may not transfer to frontier systems, and safety benchmarks get gamed; the work can provide reassurance without real control.

who_could_be_harmed: Workers in industries that depend on consumer demand; people shamed for spending they can't easily change.
dual_use: Tools that model why people over-consume are the same tools that sell to them more effectively.
bias_and_representation: Research centers rich countries; much of the world consumes too little, not too much.
ethics: Who decides what counts as 'too much', and whose purchase and usage data gets collected to find out.
morality: Is it right to treat other people's wants as a problem to fix?
devils_advocate: Consumption is how most people meet needs and find joy; framing it as a problem can moralize individual choices while the real drivers are prices, wages and business models.

who_could_be_harmed: Communities whose power grids carry data-center demand; small teams and lower-income countries that cannot afford the compute; maintainers of open tools that others depend on without supporting.
dual_use: A public list of which tools are unmaintained can point attackers at abandoned software.
bias_and_representation: The open records mostly cover large labs and public platforms like Hugging Face and GitHub, so private use and much of the world are invisible.
ethics: Who has to disclose compute and energy use, and who pays to keep shared open tools running.
morality: Is it right to keep building larger systems when their energy cost is not measured in the open, and whose needs decide what gets built?
devils_advocate: Measuring changes nothing by itself: efficiency gains tend to be spent on more use, and download or commit counts say little about real use, so a tracker can give a false sense of knowing.
